title: Training materials for the analysis of RNA-seq data generated by PI3 labs
section: Getting to know the example data set
text:
Getting to know the example data set
Here, we will work with an example RNA-seq data set with samples from Arabidopsis thaliana leaves, two different genotypes (named C and E), and three ploidy levels (2x, 4x, and 8x for genotype C; 2x and 4x for genotype E). Five biological replicates were made for each genotype and ploidy level. The scientific questions we’ll try to address are:

at the transcriptome and cell levels, what genes are differentially expressed in polyploids (4x and 8x) relative to diploids (2x)?
are sets of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) the same across genotypes, or are there genotype-specific responses?
what pathways/biological processes are affected by polyploidy?

title: 2  Data import, normalization, and exploratory analysis
text:
2.1 Obtaining the example data
In this chapter, you will learn how to read the transcript abundances produced with salmon (Patro et al. 2017) to R, normalize data using different approaches, and perform exploratory analysis on the data. At the end of this chapter, we will be able to:
We will start by loading the required packages.
In this chapter, we will start from the output of salmon (Patro et al. 2017) for all samples (2 genotypes, 3 ploidy levels; see Preface for details), produced with the nfcore/rnaseq pipeline. salmon returns one folder per sample, each containing a quant.sf file with transcript abundances.
Let’s download the example data from Zenodo and store it in a temporary directory.
# Download example data to a temporary directory
fpath <- file.path(tempdir(), "example_data.zip")
download.file(
    url = "https://zenodo.org/records/22938731/files/star_salmon.zip?download=1",
    destfile = fpath
)

# Unzip file
unzip(fpath, exdir = tempdir())
The output folder is called star_salmon. This is what it looks like:
# Check the contents of the `star_salmon` folder
salmon_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "star_salmon")

We will also need a table of sample metadata, available in the same Zenodo dataset.
# Get sample metadata from Zenodo directly to R
coldata <- read_tsv(
    "https://zenodo.org/records/22938731/files/sample_metadata.tsv?download=1",
    show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
    tibble::column_to_rownames("sample")

section: 2.2 Data import: from quant.sf files to a SummarizedExperiment object
text:
2.2 Data import: from quant.sf files to a SummarizedExperiment object
To import data from quant.sf files, we will use the tximport package (Soneson et al. 2016). For that, we need to specify the paths to all quant.sf files, as well as a table of transcript-to-gene ID mappings. This is because transcriptomics quantifies transcript abundances, but we’re often interested in analyzing data at the gene level. Hence, we need to aggregate transcript-level abundances to gene-level abundances.
There are many ways you can obtain correspondence tables between transcripts and genes (e.g., from GTF files, from headers in the FASTA files for transcripts, etc). The PLAZA database (Van Bel et al. 2022) for comparative plant genomics already provides such tables for all of its ~150 species, so we will retrieve it from there.

# Retrieve transcript-to-gene mappings from PLAZA
ath_tx2gene <- rplaza::get_id_conversions("ath") |>
    filter(alt_id_type == "tid") |>
    select(txid = alt_id, geneid = original_id)

head(ath_tx2gene)

         txid    geneid
1 AT1G01010.1 AT1G01010
2 AT1G01020.5 AT1G01020
3 AT1G01030.1 AT1G01030
4 AT1G01040.1 AT1G01040
5 AT1G01046.1 AT1G01046
6 AT1G01050.1 AT1G01050


Note that the order of the columns matter: transcript IDs must be in column 1, and their corresponding parent gene IDs in column 2. We will need the paths to all quant.sf files. This can be obtained with:

# Define paths to `quant.sf` files
qfiles <- list.files(
    salmon_dir, recursive = TRUE, pattern = "\\.sf", full.names = TRUE
)

head(qfiles)

[1] "/tmp/RtmpUNHU0q/star_salmon/C2x_rep1/quant.sf"
[2] "/tmp/RtmpUNHU0q/star_salmon/C2x_rep2/quant.sf"
[3] "/tmp/RtmpUNHU0q/star_salmon/C2x_rep3/quant.sf"
[4] "/tmp/RtmpUNHU0q/star_salmon/C2x_rep4/quant.sf"
[5] "/tmp/RtmpUNHU0q/star_salmon/C2x_rep5/quant.sf"
[6] "/tmp/RtmpUNHU0q/star_salmon/C4x_rep1/quant.sf"


With that, we can import a table of gene-level transcript abundances across samples. One of the main advantages of using tximport is that it aggregates transcript-level abundances to gene-level abundances while correcting for differences in transcript lengths (i.e., because longer transcripts tend to have more reads mapped to them). However, since we have 3’ tagged RNA-seq data, there are no differences in transcript lengths, because we didn’t sequence full transcripts. Hence, we will not correct for transcript length biases here. We can import abundances with:

# Import gene-level tx abundances across samples
counts <- tximport(
    qfiles, type = "salmon", tx2gene = ath_tx2gene, countsFromAbundance = "no"
)$counts

# Add proper column names (sample IDs)
colnames(counts) <- basename(dirname(qfiles))

# Make sure values are integers
counts <- round(counts)

In the Bioconductor ecosystem, package developers and users rely on the SummarizedExperiment class to store quantitative data and associated metadata. This ensures packages can seamless interoperate with each other, and makes data analysis workflows simpler. We can create a SummarizedExperiment object with:

# Making sure sample IDs in `coldata` match column names in `counts`
coldata <- coldata[match(rownames(coldata), colnames(counts)), ]

# Creating a `SummarizedExperiment` object
se <- SummarizedExperiment(
    assays = list(counts = counts),
    colData = coldata
)

se

class: SummarizedExperiment 
dim: 32508 25 
metadata(0):
assays(1): counts
rownames(32508): AT1G01010 AT1G01020 ... ATMG09960 ATMG09980
rowData names(0):
colnames(25): C2x_rep1 C2x_rep2 ... E4x_rep4 E4x_rep5
colData names(4): genotype ploidy genotype_ploidy spike_in
